docker-internals-deep-dive.core: Docker containers are Linux processes isolated by namespaces and limited by cgroups, running on layered union filesystems. Building well means cache-friendly layer ordering, multi-stage builds, distroless runtimes and BuildKit features, and running well means exec-form commands and proper PID 1 signal handling.

first_principles.problem: Treating containers as magic leads to bloated images, slow builds, insecure layers and broken shutdowns.

analogy.title: Shipping containers built from standard panels
analogy.story: Standard parts, minimal contents and a proper procedure for opening and closing.
analogy.breaks: Steel containers isolate physically; Linux containers share a kernel.

example.title: Production-grade image
example.outcome: containers you can trust in production.

check.q: What two kernel features make a container?

container-runtimes-docker-containerd-run.core: Containers run through a layered stack: Kubernetes → CRI (containerd/CRI-O) → shim → OCI runtime (runc). OCI standards make images portable. Because containers share the host kernel, harden them with least privilege, and use sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata, Firecracker) selected via RuntimeClass for untrusted workloads.

first_principles.problem: Without understanding the runtime stack, teams misjudge portability and isolation.

analogy.title: A logistics chain with standard containers and secure vaults
analogy.story: Standard boxes travel anywhere; valuables go in reinforced cases.
analogy.breaks: Reinforced cases are slower to handle, just as sandboxes add overhead.

example.title: Multi-tenant platform
flow: containerd with runc and runsc handlers

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Standard by default, sandboxed by need.

check.q: What interface does the kubelet use to talk to container runtimes?

webassembly-wasm-wasi-edge.core: WebAssembly brings portable, sandboxed, near-instant compute beyond the browser. WASI and the Component Model add capability-based system access and composition. Wasm complements containers: tiny and fast for edge, plugins and serverless, while containers remain best for general workloads. The developer ecosystem, led by Rust, Spin and Wasmtime, is maturing quickly.

first_principles.problem: Some workloads need faster startup, higher density and stronger isolation than containers offer.
derivation: **Deploy** at the edge or on K8s.

analogy.title: Universal cartridges for compute
analogy.story: Plug into any machine, start instantly and can't interfere with others.
analogy.breaks: Cartridges are finished products; Wasm standards are still evolving.

example.title: Plugin system
flow: SaaS lets customers upload Wasm plugins
Wasmtime runs each with no filesystem/network

check.q: What is WASI?
check.a: The WebAssembly System Interface: standard capability-based APIs letting Wasm access system resources.

unikernels-libraryos-mirageos-unikraft.core: Unikernels compile an application with only the library-OS components it needs into a single-purpose VM image. They boot in milliseconds, are tiny and have minimal attack surface with hypervisor isolation, but they're specialised. MirageOS and Unikraft lead the ecosystem, and they fit network functions, dense serverless and security-critical niches.

first_principles.problem: General-purpose OSes waste resources and widen attack surfaces for single-purpose cloud services.
truths: Apps use a small part of the OS.
Less code is faster and safer.

analogy.title: Purpose-built tools versus multi-tools
analogy.story: A dedicated tool is lighter and better at its one job.
analogy.breaks: Tools don't need patching pipelines; unikernels need rebuild-and-redeploy workflows.

check.q: What's the main trade-off of unikernels?
check.a: Specialisation: limited compatibility, tooling and debugging compared with general OSes and containers.

k8s-primitives-pods-services-deployments.core: Kubernetes' core primitives compose into most applications: Pods co-locate containers, probes report health, Services give stable discovery and load balancing, Service types control exposure, Deployments run and roll out stateless replicas, and ConfigMaps and Secrets decouple configuration from images.

first_principles.problem: Running containers at scale needs self-healing, discovery, safe rollouts and configuration management.

analogy.title: A self-managing restaurant chain
analogy.story: Kitchens (Pods), a central phone line (Service), a franchise manager (Deployment) and recipe cards (ConfigMaps).
analogy.breaks: Restaurants don't rebuild themselves overnight; Kubernetes does continuously.

example.title: Deploying a web API
flow: ConfigMap for settings, ExternalSecret for DB

check.q: Which object keeps a set number of identical Pods running and manages rollouts?

k8s-workload-management-statefulsets-dae.core: Beyond stateless Deployments, Kubernetes offers StatefulSets for stable identity and storage with ordered updates, DaemonSets for per-node agents, Jobs and CronJobs for run-to-completion and scheduled work, and PodDisruptionBudgets to keep workloads available during voluntary disruptions.

first_principles.problem: Using Deployments for everything breaks databases, node agents and batch jobs.
truths: Identity and storage matter for state.

analogy.title: Different employment contracts
analogy.story: Permanent specialists, floor wardens, contractors and shift rules.
analogy.breaks: Contracts are negotiated; controllers enforce behaviour automatically.

example.title: Data platform on K8s
flow: Kafka as StatefulSet with partitioned updates

check.q: Which controller should run a database cluster needing stable member names?

k8s-scheduling-math-qos-preemption.core: Kubernetes scheduling filters and scores nodes using requests, not usage. Requests reserve and limits cap (CPU throttles, memory OOM-kills). Bin packing and node shapes decide efficiency, DRF frames multi-resource fairness, QoS classes decide eviction order, and PriorityClasses enable preemption for important work.

first_principles.problem: Misunderstood scheduling maths causes Pending Pods, waste, unfairness and the wrong Pods being evicted.

analogy.title: Air traffic slots and seat classes
analogy.story: Slots allocated by declared need, efficient packing of planes, and priority boarding when it's full.
analogy.breaks: Passengers are counted exactly; Pod usage often diverges from requests.

check.q: What resource behaviour differs between exceeding CPU and memory limits?
check.a: CPU over limit is throttled; memory over limit is OOM-killed.

k8s-networking-cni-ingress-policies-dns.core: Kubernetes networking gives every Pod a routable IP via CNI plugins (overlay or direct routing), stable discovery via Services and CoreDNS, HTTP entry via Ingress and its successor Gateway API, and Pod-level firewalling with NetworkPolicies enforced by the CNI.

first_principles.problem: Distributed Pods need connectivity, discovery, external access and security in a constantly changing cluster.
truths: Pods are ephemeral but need addresses.

analogy.title: A city's addressing, phone book, front gates and internal security doors
analogy.story: Every flat reachable, easy to look up, guarded at the entrance and locked between zones.
analogy.breaks: Cities change slowly; Pods are created and destroyed constantly.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Connectivity, discovery, entry and security layered.

check.q: Which resource is the modern, role-oriented replacement for Ingress?
check.a: The Gateway API (Gateway and Route resources).

k8s-storage-csi-pvc-storageclass.core: Kubernetes storage separates supply from demand: PVCs request storage, StorageClasses provision PVs dynamically through CSI drivers (with WaitForFirstConsumer for zonal correctness), reclaim policies decide what happens on deletion, and snapshots and ephemeral volumes cover recovery and scratch needs.

first_principles.problem: Stateful apps on ephemeral, rescheduled Pods need persistent, correctly placed, recoverable storage.

analogy.title: A storage rental business
analogy.story: Request a unit, get one of the right type in the right location, decide what happens on cancellation, take inventory photos.
analogy.breaks: Rental units are always reachable; zonal volumes only attach in their zone.

check.q: What links a PVC to the type of storage provisioned?

k8s-control-plane-components.core: The Kubernetes control plane is a hub-and-spoke system: the API server authenticates, authorises and admits every request and persists it in etcd (a Raft-replicated store needing quorum), controllers reconcile desired and actual state, and the scheduler binds Pods to nodes via a pluggable framework.

first_principles.problem: Without understanding the control plane, failures and slowdowns are mysteries.
truths: State must be consistent and durable.

analogy.title: A head office with reception, records, managers and dispatch
analogy.story: Every request goes through reception; records are kept safe; managers and dispatchers act on them.
analogy.breaks: Offices pause at night; the control plane runs continuously.

example.title: Debugging a stuck rollout
flow: Check API server events and admission errors
Check etcd latency if everything is slow

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Know which component owns each step.

check.q: What are the three gates every API request passes?

k8s-extensibility-crds-operators-webhook.core: Kubernetes extends through CRDs (new validated resource types), controllers and operators (level-triggered reconciliation encoding expert operations, built with controller-runtime and Kubebuilder), admission webhooks or CEL policies (mutate and validate requests) and aggregated API servers for fully custom APIs.

first_principles.problem: Platforms need domain-specific automation beyond built-in objects.

analogy.title: Expanding a city's services
analogy.story: New service types registered, expert crews to run them and inspectors at the gates.
analogy.breaks: City expansions are slow; CRDs and controllers deploy in minutes.

example.title: Self-service databases
flow: Validating policy enforces sizes per namespace

check.q: What's the simplest way to add a new resource type to Kubernetes?

k8s-helm-package-manager.core: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests as charts: Go templates plus layered values render per-environment YAML, installed as versioned releases with upgrade and rollback. Charts are shared via repositories or OCI registries, should be vetted, and follow a standard layout with schema validation.

first_principles.problem: Copy-pasted YAML across environments drifts and is hard to upgrade safely.

analogy.title: A configurable product kit
analogy.story: One kit, options per customer, a delivery log and an approved supplier list.
analogy.breaks: Kits are physical; charts are code executed with your cluster permissions.

example.title: Promoting an app through environments
flow: Chart in OCI registry, version pinned

check.q: How do you roll back a Helm release?

k8s-operator-development-go-kubebuilder.core: Operator development with Kubebuilder turns runbooks into reconcile loops: scaffold types and controllers, fetch objects by key, create or update owned children idempotently, ignore deleted parents, report conditions and observedGeneration in status, and use finalizers to clean up external resources before deletion.

first_principles.problem: Naive controllers churn, duplicate resources, hide state and leak external resources.

analogy.title: Automating a meticulous caretaker
analogy.story: Checks everything each round, fixes only what's wrong, reports clearly and leaves nothing behind when the contract ends.
analogy.breaks: Caretakers use judgement; operators need explicit code for every case.

example.title: Database operator milestones
flow: v0.3: backups to S3 with finalizer cleanup

check.q: Why do operators use finalizers?
check.a: To run cleanup of external resources before Kubernetes removes the custom resource.

k8s-advanced-scheduling-affinity-taints-.core: Advanced scheduling gives placement control: taints and tolerations repel Pods from special nodes, node affinity attracts them to suitable nodes, Pod affinity and anti-affinity place Pods relative to each other, and topology spread constraints distribute replicas evenly across zones and hosts for high availability.

first_principles.problem: Naive placement wastes special capacity and concentrates failure risk.

analogy.title: Event seating strategy
analogy.story: Reserved sections, preferred areas, friends together, rivals apart and even table distribution.
analogy.breaks: Guests stay seated; Pods may need rescheduling (descheduler) to rebalance.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Combine tools for cost, performance and HA.

check.q: Which mechanism is the modern recommended way to spread replicas across zones?

k8s-multi-cluster-federation-gitops-mesh.core: Multi-cluster Kubernetes contains blast radius and meets regional, scale and compliance needs. Manage fleets with federation or GitOps (hub-and-spoke or per-cluster agents), connect services across clusters with shared-trust service meshes and the MCS API, and provision clusters declaratively with Cluster API.

first_principles.problem: One cluster can't satisfy isolation, latency and scale needs, but many clusters create consistency and connectivity problems.

analogy.title: Running a chain of branch offices
analogy.story: Standard policies, connected phone lines and a construction company that builds new branches to spec.
analogy.breaks: Branches open over months; clusters can be created in minutes.

example.title: Global platform
flow: Cluster API provisions regional clusters from ClusterClass
Flux per cluster syncs from Git

check.q: Which project manages cluster lifecycle declaratively?

k8s-security-oidc-rbac-pss.core: Kubernetes security internals: identity comes from outside (OIDC via brokers like Dex/Keycloak, short-lived service account tokens), RBAC grants additive least-privilege permissions, and Pod Security Standards (privileged, baseline, restricted) are enforced per namespace by Pod Security Admission, rolled out via warn, audit and then enforce.

first_principles.problem: Default clusters allow broad access and dangerous workloads.

analogy.title: A secure campus
analogy.story: Badges issued by HR, key rights per building and safety codes per room.
analogy.breaks: Campuses rarely change rules; cluster security must keep pace with releases.

example.title: Hardening an existing cluster
flow: Move humans to OIDC via Keycloak
Replace cluster-admin sharing with namespace RoleBindings

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Identity, authorisation and workload policy together.

check.q: How are Pod Security Standards enforced in modern Kubernetes?
check.a: By the built-in Pod Security Admission controller using namespace labels.

k8s-resource-tuning-requests-limits-auto.core: Resource tuning finds the Goldilocks zone: requests that match real usage (they drive scheduling and fairness), memory limits with headroom (to avoid OOM kills), careful CPU limits (CFS throttling causes latency), QoS classes for eviction order, and non-conflicting autoscaling with HPA, VPA and node autoscalers, all driven by measured data.

first_principles.problem: Guessed resource values waste money and cause throttling, OOMs and evictions.

analogy.title: Managing a restaurant's seating and staffing
analogy.story: Book tables realistically, set fire limits, and add staff or tables as the crowd grows.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants adjust nightly; clusters autoscale in seconds.

example.title: Cluster-wide tuning programme
flow: Deploy VPA in recommend mode everywhere
Remove CPU limits on latency services
HPA on RPS; Karpenter for nodes

check.q: What's a common recommendation for CPU limits on latency-sensitive services?
check.a: Avoid them or set them generously, relying on accurate requests, to prevent CFS throttling.

k8s-networking-internals-kubeproxy-cni-d.core: Kubernetes networking internals: Services are virtual IPs implemented by kube-proxy (iptables, IPVS, nftables) or eBPF via DNAT and conntrack on every node; CNI plugins wire Pods with veth pairs, IPAM and routes; and debugging follows the packet hop by hop, checking DNS, endpoints, rules, routing, ports and MTU.

first_principles.problem: Network issues in Kubernetes seem magical without knowing the plumbing.

analogy.title: A building's internal phone and cabling system
analogy.story: Forwarding numbers, wired extensions and a methodical way to find the broken cable.
analogy.breaks: Building cabling rarely changes; Pod networking is reconfigured constantly.

example.title: Intermittent timeouts
flow: Same-node OK, cross-node fails for large payloads

check.q: Which component programs Service translation rules on each node by default?

etcd-operations-defrag-members-disaster-.core: etcd is the cluster's sensitive brain: it needs fast disks, low-latency networking and quorum. Operate it with compaction and member-by-member defragmentation, careful membership changes (learners, one at a time), frequent off-cluster snapshots with rehearsed restores, and monitoring of fsync latency, leader changes and DB size.

first_principles.problem: etcd neglect causes slow APIs, read-only clusters or unrecoverable data loss.

analogy.title: Caring for a precision instrument
analogy.story: Calibrate it, keep it clean, service parts one at a time and keep a spare.
analogy.breaks: Instruments don't vote; etcd members must maintain quorum through every operation.

example.title: Self-managed control plane runbook
flow: Alerts on fsync and DB size

check.q: What alarm makes etcd reject writes when it runs out of space?

k8s-advanced-debugging-ephemeral-pprof-d.core: When logs aren't enough, debug Kubernetes workloads live: kubectl debug attaches ephemeral toolboxes (even to distroless Pods), profilers like pprof reveal CPU and memory hot spots, DNS tracing catches ndots, loop and timeout problems, and tcpdump in the Pod's network namespace provides packet-level ground truth.

first_principles.problem: Minimal images and ephemeral Pods make deep debugging hard.
truths: Each problem class has its tool.

analogy.title: A forensic investigation kit
analogy.story: Fingerprints, scans and recordings, gathered without disturbing the scene.
analogy.breaks: Crime scenes stay still; Pods may be rescheduled any moment, so act quickly.

example.title: Latency regression investigation
flow: DNS trace: extra lookups from ndots

check.q: Which kubectl feature lets you add a toolbox to a running Pod?

docker-compose-local-dev.core: Docker Compose declares a local multi-container stack in compose.yaml: services with health-ordered dependencies, name-based networking and isolation, named volumes for data and bind mounts for live code, all driven by a handful of commands. It's the fastest route to reproducible local environments.

first_principles.problem: Hand-run containers make local setup slow, inconsistent and fragile.
truths: Dev needs fast feedback and persistence.

analogy.title: A self-assembling model kit
analogy.story: One instruction sheet builds the whole model in the right order, every time.
analogy.breaks: Models are built once; Compose stacks are rebuilt daily.

example.title: Full local stack
flow: web + api + db + redis in compose.yaml

check.q: How do Compose services find each other?
check.a: By service name, through the project network's built-in DNS.

k8s-dashboarding-tooling-lens-k9s-krew.core: Kubernetes tooling speeds up exploration and troubleshooting: the official Dashboard (secure it carefully), Lens/Freelens as a desktop IDE, k9s for keyboard-driven terminal work, relationship views (Octant's legacy in Headlamp, kubectl tree) and Krew for kubectl plugins, while changes still flow through GitOps.

first_principles.problem: Raw kubectl is slow for navigation, and unsafe UIs create breaches.
truths: Git should remain the change path.

analogy.title: A mechanic's workshop of specialised tools
analogy.story: Diagnostic screens, hand tools and accessory kits, with dangerous equipment locked.
analogy.breaks: Workshop tools don't connect to production; these tools act on live clusters.

check.q: Which tool is a keyboard-driven terminal UI for Kubernetes?

k8s-virtual-clusters-vcluster-multi-tena.core: Virtual clusters give each tenant its own lightweight control plane inside a host namespace, with a syncer bridging low-level objects to the host for scheduling. They fill the gap between cheap-but-shared namespaces and isolated-but-costly dedicated clusters, ideal for dev sandboxes, CI and platform tenancy.

first_principles.problem: Teams need cluster-level autonomy without the cost of separate clusters.

analogy.title: Flats inside one building
analogy.story: Each tenant has their own front door and rules, sharing the building's structure and utilities.
analogy.breaks: Flats have physical walls; virtual clusters share kernels unless sandboxed.

example.title: Internal developer platform
flow: Each team gets a vCluster with admin rights

check.q: What component copies Pods from a virtual cluster to the host cluster?

service-mesh-internals-envoy-wasm-inject.core: Service mesh internals: Envoy proxies (sidecars or ambient ztunnel/waypoints) receive layered config (listeners, filters, routes, clusters, endpoints) via xDS from a control plane, process requests through ordered filter chains extensible with Wasm, are injected by mutating webhooks, intercept traffic with iptables redirection and are debugged with istioctl and response flags.

first_principles.problem: Meshes add powerful features but are opaque without understanding their engine room.
truths: Injection and redirection are mechanisms with failure modes.

analogy.title: The engine room of a ship
analogy.story: Many interlocking machines, instructions from the bridge and gauges that tell you what's wrong.
analogy.breaks: Ship engines are physical; mesh config changes live in seconds.

example.title: Rolling out a mesh
flow: Istio CNI to avoid NET_ADMIN init

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Understand the machinery before relying on it.

check.q: What injects the Envoy sidecar into Pods in Istio?
check.a: A mutating admission webhook served by istiod.

k8s-keda-event-driven-autoscaling.core: KEDA brings event-driven autoscaling to Kubernetes: scalers read real demand signals (queue depth, lag, Prometheus queries, cron), the operator scales workloads to and from zero, a KEDA-managed HPA handles 1→N, ScaledObjects declare targets and fallbacks, and TriggerAuthentication supplies credentials securely.

first_principles.problem: CPU-based scaling misses backlog and can't scale idle workloads to zero.

analogy.title: Smart staffing driven by the real queue
analogy.story: Staff arrive when orders arrive and go home when the queue is empty.
analogy.breaks: Staff arrive instantly; Pods need startup time.

example.title: Event-driven worker fleet
flow: Cron trigger for business hours APIs

check.q: What does KEDA add beyond standard HPA?
check.a: External event-based metrics via scalers and the ability to scale to and from zero.

k8s-runtime-classes-gvisor-kata.core: Runtime classes let clusters mix isolation levels: hardened runc for trusted workloads and sandboxed runtimes (gVisor's user-space kernel or Kata's per-Pod VMs) for untrusted code. RuntimeClass maps names to node handlers with overhead and scheduling, Pods opt in with runtimeClassName, and policies enforce it for tenants.

first_principles.problem: Shared-kernel containers are risky for untrusted, multi-tenant workloads.

analogy.title: Different security zones in a facility
analogy.story: Open offices, badge-controlled labs and sealed cleanrooms, each for the right people.
analogy.breaks: Facilities have physical walls; sandboxes are software and hardware boundaries with their own CVEs.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Isolation by default for the untrusted.

check.q: Which Pod field selects a sandboxed runtime?

k8s-api-aggregation-layer.core: The API aggregation layer lets kube-apiserver proxy whole API groups to extension API servers registered by APIService objects, with delegated authentication (trusted front-proxy headers) and authorisation (SubjectAccessReview). metrics-server is the canonical example. Use it only when CRDs can't meet storage, computation or scale needs.

first_principles.problem: Some APIs need behaviour or storage beyond what CRDs in etcd provide.

analogy.title: Concessions inside a department store
analogy.story: Specialist counters operate behind the store's front door, under its security.
analogy.breaks: Concessions are visible to shoppers; aggregated APIs look native to clients.

check.q: Which object registers an aggregated API with kube-apiserver?
